title: Form, Structure, and Sense, Part 1: Method and Two Questions

beats.say: These questions test grammar inside a sentence. They ask you to match verbs to subjects, choose the right tense, match pronouns, form possessives, and place modifiers.
The question is always the same: which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
The best habit is to look at the choices first, and see which rule is being tested.

card.text: Look at what changes in the choices

beats.say: Step one. Look at the choices, and see what's changing. Is it a singular or plural verb, a tense, a pronoun, an apostrophe, or the word order?
beats.item: See what changes in the choices

beats.say: Step two. For agreement, cross out phrases that begin with of, in, or with. The true subject is never inside them.
Step three. For tense, find the time clue in the sentence. A date or a word like currently tells you the tense.
Step four. For a modifier, ask who or what's doing the action. That noun must come right after the comma.
A singular subject takes a singular verb, which often ends in s. The list of names is long.
Collective nouns such as team, committee, and collection are singular. The committee has voted.
The past perfect, had plus a past participle, shows an action before another past action. By nineteen hundred, the canal had closed.
A pronoun must match its noun in number. The museum reopened its doors, not their doors.
A singular possessive is city apostrophe s. A plural that ends in s is cities apostrophe. An irregular plural is children apostrophe s.
Easy question. We find the true subject by crossing out the phrases that sit between the subject and the verb.

scenes.title: Read the sentence
scenes.text: The set of instructions included with the new bookshelves ______ several diagrams that show how each panel fits together.

beats.say: Cross out of instructions, and included with the new bookshelves. Those phrases only describe the subject.
What remains is, the set, blank, several diagrams. The subject is the set, which is singular, so we need a singular verb.

scenes.title: Which verb fits?
scenes.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

beats.say: Choice A, contain, is a plural form. It would agree with instructions, but instructions isn't the subject.
Choice C, have contained, is plural too. It doesn't agree with the set.
Choice D, are containing, is also plural, so it can't agree with a singular subject.
Choice B, contains, is singular, and agrees with the set. The answer is B.
Medium question. An opening phrase describes the first noun after the comma. That noun must be the person or thing doing the action.

scenes.title: Read the sentence
scenes.text: Carefully restored over three years by a team of conservators, ______

beats.say: The opening phrase is carefully restored over three years. Something was restored.
The thing that was restored must come right after the comma. In this story, that's the painting, not the team and not the hall.

scenes.title: Which sentence is correct?
scenes.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

options.A: the team returned the painting to the gallery's main hall in 2022.
options.B: the gallery's main hall received the painting again in 2022.
options.C: the painting returned to the gallery's main hall in 2022.
options.D: the conservators' work was displayed in the gallery's main hall in 2022.

beats.say: Choice A puts the team right after the comma. But the team did the restoring, it wasn't restored.
Choice B puts the main hall right after the comma. The hall wasn't restored either.
Choice D puts the conservators' work after the comma. The work wasn't restored, the painting was.
Choice C puts the painting right after the comma, so the modifier points to the right noun. The answer is C.
To recap. Look at the choices to see which rule is tested. Cross out phrases to find the true subject.
beats.item: See the rule; find the subject

beats.say: Use the time clue for tense, and put the doer right after an opening phrase. In the next video, we work through a hard question and the common traps.
